title: Pseudepigrapha in the New Testament
subtitle: Books written in another's name — the scholarly debate over New Testament authorship, the case of 2 Peter, and how two traditions police attribution
summary: Several New Testament letters name an apostle as author even though many scholars question that attribution. The strongest disputes concern letters such as 2 Peter and some Pauline epistles; other books remain widely accepted as authentic. The issue is not whether all Christian scripture is fabricated, but whether writings of uncertain authorship can bear the same claim of protected revelation as a publicly transmitted prophetic recitation.

seo.metaTitle: Pseudepigrapha in the New Testament: The 2 Peter Question
seo.metaDescription: Several New Testament letters name an apostle as author even though many scholars question that attribution.

sections.title: The Evidence in Brief
sections.body: Several New Testament letters name apostles as authors, while many scholars question some attributions. The main disputes concern 2 Peter and some Pauline letters. This does not mean all Christian scripture is fabricated. It raises a focused question. Can a text with uncertain authorship carry the same certainty as public prophetic revelation?

sections.title: In Brief
sections.body: Pseudepigraphy means writing in another person’s name. Most scholars accept seven Pauline letters. Ephesians, Colossians, and 2 Thessalonians are disputed. The Pastoral Epistles are often dated after Paul. 2 Peter is the clearest disputed case. These judgments do not prove every book false. They do make authorship important when revelation is claimed.

sections.title: Writing in Another’s Name in the Ancient World
sections.body:
Writing under a revered name existed in the ancient world. Scholars debate whether every audience saw it as fraud. The early church rejected some works because it judged their apostolic names false. Serapion rejected the Gospel of Peter. The Muratorian Fragment rejects letters falsely linked to Paul.

2 Thessalonians 2:1–2 warns about a letter presented as apostolic. 3:17 gives a handwritten sign. Whether the letter is Pauline remains debated. The warning shows that false attribution was a real concern.

sections.title: The Three Tiers of the Pauline Letters
sections.body:
The thirteen letters bearing Paul’s name fall into groups. Romans, 1–2 Corinthians, Galatians, Philippians, 1 Thessalonians, and Philemon are widely accepted as Pauline. Ephesians, Colossians, and 2 Thessalonians are disputed. Many critical scholars date 1–2 Timothy and Titus after Paul.

The debate concerns vocabulary, style, church order, theology, and Paul’s known life. Conservative scholars cite coauthors, secretaries, changing topics, and a later ministry. The majority view matters. It remains a historical conclusion, not a mathematical proof.

sections.title: The Case of 2 Peter: The Critical Argument
sections.body:
2 Peter is often judged pseudonymous. Its Greek differs from 1 Peter. It reworks much of Jude. It addresses concern about Christ’s delayed return. It appears to know a collection of Paul’s letters as Scripture (2 Peter 3:15–16). Many scholars therefore place it after Peter’s death.

These arguments are serious, but not all are decisive. Style can change. Borrowing does not prove a late date. Richard Bauckham accepts a late first-century setting and reads the book as a literary testament. The critical case deserves attention. Its exact date and intention remain debated.

sections.title: The Conservative Case for 2 Peter
sections.body:
Defenders of Peter’s authorship offer replies. A different secretary could explain the Greek style. Jude may have borrowed from 2 Peter, or both may use shared material. “The fathers” may mean Old Testament patriarchs. Early caution may reflect limited circulation.

2 Peter 1:16 presents its author as an eyewitness. Defenders accept this claim. Critics answer that pseudonymous works also use strong self-authentication. The defense deserves to be heard. It does not remove the reasons many specialists and early Christians hesitated.

sections.title: An Islamic Lens: Writing a Text and Calling It God’s
sections.body:
Quran 2:79 condemns writing a text and then saying, “This is from Allah.” The verse addresses particular misconduct. It still gives an Islamic principle. Claims about God require trustworthy transmission.

The Quran was recited publicly. It was memorized and written during Muhammad’s life. It was collected soon after his death. It was standardized within the first Muslim generation. Quran 15:9 declares God’s protection. No Quranic book has a prophetic author rejected by most specialists.

Muslims also graded hadith. Scholars recorded chains. They studied narrators. They compared wording. They marked reports as authentic, weak, or fabricated. This separates the mass-transmitted Quran from reports needing individual authentication.

sections.title: Where Each Tradition Locates Its Guaranteed Core
sections.body:
The traditions locate certainty differently. Christianity places disputed-attribution books inside its canon. Christians defend traditional authorship or place inspiration in the text recognized by the church. Early churches sometimes rejected books because they believed their apostolic names were false.

Islam places guaranteed scripture in one public Quran transmitted in the first generation. Hadith can be authoritative when authenticated. Individual reports can also be rejected without removing a Quranic verse. Muslims say the Quran’s mass recitation and early manuscripts support the compilation reports.

This does not prove every disputed Christian book false. It does show why the Islamic model gives clear public grounds for identifying revelation.

sections.title: Why This Matters: Pseudepigrapha in the New Testament
sections.body: Many scholars question the apostolic authorship of 2 Peter and the Pastoral Epistles. Conservative defenses remain. The evidence should not be exaggerated. The comparison still favors Islam’s model. The Quran was public and early. Hadith reports were named, tested, and graded. They were not automatically treated as scripture.

faq.question: What exactly does “pseudepigrapha” mean?
faq.answer: From Greek, it means “falsely inscribed” writings — works composed by one person but circulated under the name of another, usually a revered figure. In New Testament studies the term (or “pseudonymity”) describes the scholarly view that some canonical books carry apostolic names their actual authors did not bear.

faq.question: Do all scholars agree that 2 Peter was not written by Peter?
faq.answer: No. Most critical scholars judge it pseudonymous — J. N. D. Kelly’s line that “scarcely anyone nowadays doubts” it is often quoted — but the verdict is contested. Michael Kruger, E. M. B. Green, and the textbook of Carson and Moo defend Petrine authorship, and Richard Bauckham holds a mediating view: a late-first-century “testament” whose original readers would have recognized the genre.

faq.question: If the early church doubted 2 Peter, why is it in the Bible?
faq.answer: The doubts were eventually weighed and set aside: Athanasius’s Easter letter of 367 and the late-fourth-century councils received it among the seven Catholic Epistles. Defenders read that history as evidence of careful scrutiny rather than credulity; critical scholars read it as a late decision made without the linguistic and historical tools available today. Both readings of the same facts are represented in current scholarship.

faq.question: Which Pauline letters does mainstream scholarship consider genuine?
faq.answer: Seven are undisputed: Romans, 1 and 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Philippians, 1 Thessalonians, and Philemon. Ephesians, Colossians, and 2 Thessalonians are seriously disputed, with scholars on both sides. Most critical scholars regard the Pastorals (1-2 Timothy, Titus) as written in Paul’s name after his death — a majority view that conservative scholarship contests in detail.

faq.question: Does Islam have an equivalent problem of false attribution?
faq.answer: False attribution occurred in hadith literature, and Muslim scholars said so openly. The difference is structural: fabricated or weak hadith are not part of the Quran and can be rejected through hadith criticism without removing a verse from scripture. The Quran was a public recitation collected and standardized in the first generation, with early manuscript and mass-transmission evidence. Islam therefore has a serious history of disputed reports, but not a direct equivalent of a canonical Quranic chapter that most specialists attribute to someone other than its claimed apostolic author.

faq.question: If a biblical book is pseudonymous, does that make it worthless or Christianity false?
faq.answer: Not by itself. A pseudonymity verdict is a historical judgment about human authorship, and Christian theologians hold a range of positions on how inspiration relates to that question — from denying the verdicts outright to arguing that canonical authority does not depend on modern authorship verification. What the debate does affect is the argument that canonicity guarantees apostolic authorship; each reader must weigh how much rests on that link.

furtherReading.title: Forgery and Counterforgery: The Use of Literary Deceit in Early Christian Polemics
furtherReading.author: Bart D. Ehrman
furtherReading.note: The fullest modern statement of the critical case that early Christian pseudepigraphy was forgery in the ancient world’s own terms.

furtherReading.title: Jude, 2 Peter (Word Biblical Commentary 50)
furtherReading.author: Richard Bauckham
furtherReading.note: The standard technical commentary; argues for a first-century date and reads 2 Peter as a “testament” whose pseudonymity was a transparent convention.

furtherReading.title: An Introduction to the New Testament
furtherReading.author: D. A. Carson and Douglas J. Moo
furtherReading.note: The leading conservative textbook; defends traditional authorship of the disputed letters, including 2 Peter and the Pastorals.
